Commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on surah 77, verses 1–7:

(p-6019) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Mursalat (the chapter of "The Sent Forth"), also called Surat al-ʿUrf (the chapter of "Successive"). It is Meccan and has fifty verses.

Al-Bukhari related from ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah in a cave at Mina, the surah (al-Mursalat) was revealed to him. He was reciting it, and I was receiving it directly from his mouth, and his mouth was moist with it, when a snake sprang at us. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Kill it.' We rushed at it, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It has been spared your evil, just as you have been spared its evil.'" Muslim also transmitted it.

Imam Ahmad related from Ibn ʿAbbas, from his mother, that she "heard the Prophet (ﷺ) reciting al-Mursalat ʿurfan in the Maghrib (prayer)." The two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) also related it.

(p-6020) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion of the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He:

[1–7] ﴿By those sent forth successively,﴾ ﴿by those that blow violently with vehemence,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 2] ﴿and those that spread widely,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 3] ﴿and those that separate decisively,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 4] ﴿and those that deliver a reminder,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 5] ﴿as an excuse or a warning,﴾ [al-Mursalat: 6] ﴿indeed what you are promised is surely to occur.﴾ [al-Mursalat: 7]

﴿By those sent forth successively﴾: this is an oath by the winds sent in succession, like the hair of a mane (ʿurf). Or it is an oath by the angels sent by Allah's command and prohibition, and that is the ʿurf. Or it is an oath by the messengers from among the children of Adam who were sent with that.

﴿Those that blow violently with vehemence﴾ [al-Mursalat: 2]: that is, the winds that blow very strongly and pass swiftly.

﴿And those that spread widely﴾ [al-Mursalat: 3]: that is, the winds that scatter the clouds and the rain, as He said: ﴿And it is He who sends the winds as good tidings before His mercy﴾ [al-Araf: 57], and His saying: ﴿Allah is the One who sends the winds, and they stir up clouds, and He spreads them across the sky﴾ [al-Rum: 48]. Or it is the angels who spread the laws, knowledge, wisdom, prophethood and guidance upon the earth.

﴿And those that separate decisively﴾ [al-Mursalat: 4]: that is, the angels who distinguish between truth and falsehood by the sending down of revelation and the Revelation. Or the Quranic verses that similarly distinguish. Or the clouds which spread out the dead land, and so separate between those who thank Allah, exalted is He, and those who disbelieve,

(p-6021) like His saying: ﴿That We might give them abundant water to drink﴾ [al-Jinn: 16], ﴿that We might test them therein﴾ [al-Jinn: 17].

﴿And those that deliver a reminder﴾ [al-Mursalat: 5]: that is, the angels who convey the reminder of Allah to His prophets, the ones who transmit His revelation.

﴿As an excuse or a warning﴾ [al-Mursalat: 6]: that is, an excuse from Allah to His creation and a warning from Him to them. Both are verbal nouns meaning "excusing" and "warning." That is, those who deliver the reminder for the sake of excusing and warning, namely for the removal of their excuse and their being warned of the punishment of Allah, exalted is He, if they disobey His command.

﴿Indeed what you are promised is surely to occur﴾ [al-Mursalat: 7]: this is the answer to the oath. That is, what you are promised of the coming of the Resurrection and the recompense is surely going to happen and descend. Like His saying: ﴿And indeed the Judgment is surely to occur﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 6]. Or it refers to the vanishing of what you are upon of falsehood and the victory of the truth over it. Or it is more general than that. The first is preferable, because it is followed by its signs, in His saying:

The discourse on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[25–26] ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26]

﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26]. Ibn Jarir said: that is, a container (wi'a'). One says: "This is the kifat (receptacle) of this, and its kafiyah (container)," when it is its container. The meaning is: Have We not made the earth a receptacle for your living and your dead, gathering your living in dwellings and homes, so that it holds and gathers them, and your dead in its bellies, in graves, where they are buried? It is also possible that by His words ﴿a receptacle﴾ ﴿for the living and the dead﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26] He meant that it gathers their harm during their lives and their carrion after their deaths. End of quotation.

As for al-kifat (الكِفات, "receptacle"), it may be an ism jins (generic noun) for that which gathers and grasps. One says: "God took him to Himself (kafatahu Allahu ilayh)," meaning He seized him. For this reason the graveyard was called kaftah and kifat. From the same root come al-dimam (gathering) and al-jima' (assembly), for that which gathers and collects. One says: "This chapter is the jima' of the chapters."

It may be an ism alah (noun of instrument), since the pattern fi'al frequently has this function, as in this case. Or it may be a masdar (verbal noun) like qital, interpreted as a derived noun and used as an adjective, like rajulun 'adl (a just man). Or it may be the plural of kafit, like sa'im and siyam. Or it may be kift, with a kasra and then a sukun, like qidh and qidah.

﴿Kifatan﴾ is in the accusative as the second object (maf'ul thani) of "naj'al" (We made), since it is used in the sense of making something become. And ﴿ahyaan wa amwatan﴾ [al-Mursalat: 26] are in the accusative as objects of "kifatan."

Al-Shihab said: This is clear if "kifatan" is a masdar or the plural of kafit, but not if it is an ism alah, for it does not govern, as the grammarians have stated. In that case a verb is to be supposed that governs it from its own root, as Ibn Malik stated concerning every accusative noun that follows a non-governing noun. There are other possibilities.

(p-6025)

Note: In al-Iklil, al-Kiya al-Harrasi said: By the kifat he meant gathering together, and his intention is that it gathers them in both states. This indicates the obligation of covering the dead so that nothing of them is seen. Ibn Abd al-Barr said: Ibn al-Qasim argued for the amputation of the hand of the grave-robber (nabbash) from this verse, because He, exalted is He, made the grave for the dead like a house for the living, so it is a protected place (hirz).

Al-Qaffal transmitted this from Rabi'a. In my view, this kind of argument is an extreme in deduction and a forced search for something to support the school being followed, whatever it may be, which is considered arbitrariness and partisan bias. The gap between the sense of the verse and this deduction is like the gap between one who rescues and one who is accused. Similar is what some have taken from the preceding verse, ﴿For what day has it been postponed?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 12], as the postponement of judges for litigants in court proceedings, so that the judgment falls due when the postponement is complete, as al-Iklil transmitted from Ibn al-Faras. The sources of religion and legislation are not riddles or enigmas. And success is with God.

**The interpretation of His saying, Exalted is He:**

[30–40] ﴿Depart toward a shade of three branches﴾ ﴿Neither shady nor sufficient against the blaze﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 31] ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a castle﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 32] ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 33] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 34] ﴿This is a Day they will not speak﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 35] ﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuse﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 36] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 37] ﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 38] ﴿So if you have a plot, then plot against Me﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 39] ﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 40]

﴿Depart toward a shade of three branches﴾: that is, three groups (*firaq*). This refers to the smoke of Hell rising from its fuel. When it ascends, it divides into three branches because of its great size.

Al-Shihab said: In this there is a sarcastic metaphor (*isti'ara tahakkumiyya*), comparing the smoke that rises up to a shade, and there is an innovative usage (*ibda'*), because a shade does not rise above the thing that casts it.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Neither shady﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 31] is a mockery of them, because a shade is necessarily shady, that is, providing shade. Negating it of that smoke indicates that calling it a shade is a mockery of them. It also addresses the possibility that someone might imagine it brings them some relief, so He negated this supposition by His saying: ﴿Neither shady nor sufficient against the blaze﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 31], meaning that it does not ward off from them any of the flame of the Fire. The meaning is that it does not shade them from its heat, nor shelter them from its blaze.

﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks like a castle﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 32]: that is, it hurls every spark, which is as large as a castle. *Al-qasr* is the singular of *al-qusur* (castles).

Ibn Jarir said: The Arabs compare camels to built castles, as al-Akhtal said describing a she-camel:

*As if she were a Roman tower, built up with mortar, bricks and stones.*

Then he said: It has been said, "like *al-qasr*" [singular], and not "like *al-qusur*" [plural]. *Al-sharar* is a collective noun, as in His saying: ﴿The host will be routed and will turn their backs﴾ [Al-Qamar: 45], where He did not say *al-adbar*, since *al-dubur* carries the sense of *al-adbar*. He did this to harmonize the verse endings (*ru'us al-ayi*, the rhyme-endings of verses) and the ends of the phrases, because the Arabs do this and the Qur'an was revealed in their tongue.

﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 33]. It has been recited as *jimalatun* [ـمالات], the plural of *jimal* (plural of *jamal*, camel), or the plural of *jimalah*, the plural of *jamal* also. Its parallel is *rijal* and *rijalat* (men), *buyut* and *buyutat* (houses), and *hijarah* and *hijarat* (stones).

﴿Yellow﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 33] (*suffr*): that is, in color, for sparks, because of their fiery nature, are yellowish. It has also been said that *suffr* means black.

Qatada and others said: that is, like black she-camels. Ibn Jarir preferred this, claiming it is the well-known usage in the speech of the Arabs.

﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 34]. ﴿This is a Day they will not speak﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 35]: that is, they will not speak with a proof, or they will not speak at some moments of it, because it is a long day with many stations and periods. Or their speech is made as though it were no speech, because it benefits them not and is not heard. Thus this does not contradict the verses: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 23], ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [An-Nisa': 42], and ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute﴾ [Az-Zumar: 31].

﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuse﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 36]: that is, permission to offer an excuse will not be granted to them, because their excuses will not be accepted, since the proof has been established against them. He did not say *fa-ya'taziru* (and they make excuse) but *fa-ya'taziru* [with the verb in the form that rhymes], in observance of the verse endings. It has also been said: it is coordinated with "is permitted" (*yu'dhanu*) and included with it in the scope of negation, and the meaning is: there will be no permission and no excuse following it, without the excuse being made a consequence of the permission.

﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 37]. ﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 38]: that is, the truth between the servants. "We have gathered you" means We have assembled you therein, "and the former peoples" means of the destroyed nations.

﴿So if you have a plot﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 39]: that is, a scheme to escape the punishment. ﴿then plot against Me﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 39]: that is, then devise a stratagem against it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a rebuke to them for their plotting against the religion of God and its adherents, and a recording against them of their helplessness and submission.

It has been recited as *jimalatun* [ـمالات], the plural of *jimal* (plural of *jamal*, camel), or the plural of *jimalah*, the plural of *jamal* also. Its parallel is *rijal* and *rijalat* (men), *buyut* and *buyutat* (houses), and *hijarah* and *hijarat* (stones).

﴿Yellow﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 33] (*suffr*): that is, in color, for sparks, because of their fiery nature, are yellowish. It has also been said that *suffr* means black.

Qatada and others said: that is, like black she-camels. Ibn Jarir preferred this, claiming it is the well-known usage in the speech of the Arabs.

﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 34]. ﴿This is a Day they will not speak﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 35]: that is, they will not speak with a proof, or they will not speak at some moments of it, because it is a long day with many stations and periods. Or their speech is made as though it were no speech, because it benefits them not and is not heard. Thus this does not contradict the verses: ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [Al-An'am: 23], ﴿and they will not conceal from God any statement﴾ [An-Nisa': 42], and ﴿Then indeed, on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord you will dispute﴾ [Az-Zumar: 31].

﴿Nor will they be permitted to make excuse﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 36]: that is, permission to offer an excuse will not be granted to them, because their excuses will not be accepted, since the proof has been established against them. He did not say *fa-ya'taziru* (and they make excuse) but *fa-ya'taziru* [with the verb in the form that rhymes], in observance of the verse endings. It has also been said: it is coordinated with "is permitted" (*yu'dhanu*) and included with it in the scope of negation, and the meaning is: there will be no permission and no excuse following it, without the excuse being made a consequence of the permission.

﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 37]. ﴿This is the Day of Decision; We have gathered you and the former peoples﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 38]: that is, the truth between the servants. "We have gathered you" means We have assembled you therein, "and the former peoples" means of the destroyed nations.

﴿So if you have a plot﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 39]: that is, a scheme to escape the punishment. ﴿then plot against Me﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 39]: that is, then devise a stratagem against it.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is a rebuke to them for their plotting against the religion of God and its adherents, and a recording against them of their helplessness and submission.

﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 40]: that is, for they have no stratagem to ward off the punishment.

﴿Indeed, the righteous﴾ means those who guard against God's punishment by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions. ﴿Among shade﴾ means shelters from heat and cold. ﴿And springs﴾ means rivers flowing through trees.

﴿And fruit from whatever they desire﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 42] means what they long for. It is said to them: ﴿"Eat and drink with satisfaction for what you used to do."﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 43] ﴿Indeed, We thus reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 44] means in their obedience, their worship and their deeds.

﴿Woe, that Day, to the deniers!﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 45] ﴿"Eat and enjoy yourselves briefly; indeed, you are criminals."﴾ [Al-Mursalat: 46] means your portion is the portion of one who committed crime, which is eating and enjoying yourselves for a few days, and then remaining in destruction forever.

The commentary of al-Qasimi (Mahasin al-Ta'wil) on verses 47–50:

The discussion of His saying, the Exalted:

[47–50] ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48] ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 49] ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 50]

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾ [al-Mursalat: 48]. That is: submit to this truth that has been revealed, humble yourselves to accept it, and be humbled before its remembrance. "They do not bow down," that is: they do not submit, do not yield, and do not accept, out of arrogance and pride.

﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾ [al-Mursalat: 49]. That is: those who denied the messengers of God, rejecting what they conveyed to them of God's command and His prohibition. The repetition of the verse "Woe on that Day to the deniers" is for emphasis, and this is one of the common purposes of repetition. It has been said: there is no repetition, because the object of each of them differs. The full discussion has already been given in Surah (al-Rahman), so refer to it at its conclusion.

﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 50]. That is: after this Qur'an, if they deny it, despite the clarity of its proof and the soundness of its evidences, that it is a truth sent down from Him, the Exalted. In this is an admonition that there is no statement that equals it in excellence or comes near to it, let alone surpasses or exceeds it. Therefore no statement is more deserving of belief than it.
